broad.question: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

final_hypothesis.label: C4

source_paper.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The finding from the paper that a CrTaO4-based oxide forms and contributes to the oxidation resistance of NV1, with non-stoichiometry being an important factor.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: Proposes specifically tuning the alloy’s Ta content to optimize the formation of a non-stoichiometric CrTaO4, thus providing a self-healing mechanism not directly explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Increasing the refractory element Ta content will promote formation of a non‐stoichiometric CrTaO4 phase that more effectively accommodates excess Al and Cr, thereby creating a denser, self‐healing oxide scale that limits oxygen ingress at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A typical high-entropy refractory alloy containing Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti, such as the NV1 alloy with its as-cast dendritic microstructure and element segregation.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by increasing the Ta content (e.g., by ~10% relative to the baseline) while keeping other elements constant.
hypothesis.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests at high temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C) for durations of 100–200 hours in air.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a non-stoichiometric CrTaO4-based oxide that forms a continuous, low-porosity scale.
hypothesis.mechanism: Enhanced Ta availability promotes the formation of a CrTaO4 phase with altered lattice parameters that can incorporate additional Al and Cr. This modification suppresses the formation of discrete, less-protective oxides (e.g. Al2O3 or Cr2O3) and minimizes porosity by balancing cation diffusion. The denser oxide reduces both outward diffusion of reactive species and inward oxygen diffusion, yielding superior oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Ta-enhanced alloy is expected to show lower mass gains (smaller oxidation weight gain) and a more uniform and denser surface oxide layer under identical high-temperature exposure conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: The original NV1 alloy as described in PMC6513993, which forms a primarily CrTaO4-based oxide layer that becomes denser at 1100 °C but has some porosity and heterogeneous features.
hypothesis.boundary: Works in high-temperature regimes (around 1100 °C) and long-term exposures (≥100 hours), but may not be effective under very rapid cycling or at much lower temperatures where diffusion kinetics are significantly diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and the optimum Ta content require experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline composition and one with increased Ta content. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours under identical conditions.
measurements: Thermogravimetric measurements (mass gain curves) over time.
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide scale density and continuity.
Phase identification via XRD to check for non-stoichiometric CrTaO4 formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ta-enhanced alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and the oxide scale does not demonstrate increased density and continuity compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: The Effect of Fe Addition in the RM(Nb)IC Alloy Nb-30Ti-10Si-2Al-5Cr-3Fe-5Sn-2Hf (at.%) on Its Microstructure, Complex Concentrated and High Entropy Phases, Pest Oxidation, Strength and Contamination with Oxygen, and a Comparison with Other RM(Nb)ICs, Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys (RCCAs) and Refractory High Entropy Alloys (RHEAs).

top3.builds_on: the established role of reactive elements in enhancing oxide scale adhesion in superalloys and stainless steels.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the concept of reactive element effects—commonly used in conventional high-temperature alloys—to high-entropy alloys, providing a novel route for improving oxidation resistance via microstructural modification at the oxide scale interface.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor additions of a reactive element such as yttrium (Y) to high‐entropy alloys will improve the adhesion and stability of the protective oxide layer by modifying grain boundary characteristics in the oxide scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A baseline HEA similar to those studied in refractory systems that, when oxidized, develop a scale (e.g., with Sn-rich A15 features) that may suffer from spallation due to insufficient adhesion.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate a trace amount (approximately 0.2 at.%) of yttrium into the HEA composition while keeping the major alloying elements constant.
hypothesis.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at around 800 °C for a duration of 100 h.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A protective oxide scale enriched in yttrium at grain boundaries, leading to reduced void formation and improved interfacial adhesion between the oxide and the underlying substrate.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium, a well-known reactive element in oxidation-resistant alloys, segregates to oxide grain boundaries and interfaces, lowering the surface energy and promoting stronger bonds between oxide grains. This leads to a more continuous, adherent oxide scale with improved resistance to mechanical disruption and spallation. The enhanced adhesion slows down oxygen transport into the substrate, thereby improving the alloy's oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-modified HEA should show a reduced oxide spallation rate, lower mass gain during oxidation, and a more uniformly adherent, crack-free oxide scale. Microstructural analyses would reveal Y enrichment at the oxide’s grain boundaries.
hypothesis.baseline: The HEA without any reactive element addition, which displays a protective oxide layer that is more prone to spalling and non-uniform growth.
hypothesis.boundary: The reactive element mechanism is expected to be effective in high-temperature oxidizing environments (≈700–900 °C) and with very low Y additions that do not alter the overall alloy phase stability.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of yttrium for maximum improvement without affecting the HEA’s desirable mechanical properties is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one baseline HEA and one with 0.2 at.% Y added. Oxidize both sets at 800 °C for 100 h. Assess the oxide scale adhesion and microstructural characteristics using SEM/EPMA, and measure oxidation mass gain.
measurements: Mass gain kinetics
Microscopic evaluation of oxide scale morphology and spallation events
Chemical mapping to detect Y segregation at the oxide scale grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Y does not result in improved oxide adhesion (i.e., similar or increased spallation and no evident Y enrichment at critical interfaces) or if the oxidation mass gain is not significantly lower than that of the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior of Dual-Phase High Entropy Alloy for Concentrating Solar Power Systems.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s identification of phase-specific work function differences and associated micro-galvanic corrosion effects which imply that the noble FCC (L12) phase is more resistant to oxidation.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores the role of engineered microstructure—specifically altering the FCC/BCC phase balance—as a mechanistic pathway to achieve improved oxidation resistance through a more continuous protective scale, an approach not directly reported in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A higher volume fraction of the more noble FCC (L12) phase in dual-phase high-entropy alloys governs the development of a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy comprising a dual-phase microstructure with both FCC (L12) and BCC (B2) phases in its as-cast state.
hypothesis.intervention: Process the alloy (via controlled heat treatment or minor composition adjustment) to increase the relative volume fraction of the FCC (L12) phase without altering the overall elemental composition significantly.
hypothesis.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests in air at 650–750 °C, where diffusion-controlled oxidation and microstructural stability are critical, performed on samples with modified microstructural phase fractions versus a baseline alloy.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The connectivity and continuity of the FCC phase which forms a more noble and oxidation-resistant barrier, compared to the more reactive BCC phase that acts as a micro-anodic site.
hypothesis.mechanism: During oxidation, the noble FCC (L12) phase preferentially forms a stable oxide layer owing to its higher work function, while the reactive BCC (B2) phase tends to dissolve or form nonprotective oxides. Increasing the FCC phase fraction reduces the local galvanic coupling effects that otherwise accelerate oxidation at phase boundaries. This shift provides a more coherent and continuous oxide scale that protects the underlying metal.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a higher FCC volume fraction are expected to display a lower oxidation rate (e.g., reduced weight gain and scale spallation) and a more uniform oxide layer, as evidenced by microstructural and compositional analyses (optical/SEM imaging, EBSD mapping) relative to the baseline alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with an original FCC:BCC ratio (e.g., ~77:23 as reported in the paper).
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable under high-temperature oxidation environments (650–750 °C) where the stability of the dual-phase microstructure is maintained; may not extend to conditions where phase transformations dominate.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The critical FCC volume fraction threshold for optimum oxidation protection is not known precisely and may depend on other simultaneous microstructural variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one processed to have an increased FCC phase fraction (e.g., via a tailored heat-treatment schedule) and one baseline sample with the original phase fraction. Expose both to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., air at 700 °C for 50 hours), then compare oxide layer uniformity, spallation tendency, and overall oxidation rate via weight gain and microstructural characterizations.
measurements: Phase fraction analysis (using EBSD)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/XRD)
Weight gain measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased FCC phase fraction does not demonstrate a lower oxidation rate and improved oxide scale continuity compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

Calculations of Al activities with TCHEA 3.0 database in Thermo-Calc software (version 2018b) revealed the Al activity of NV1 alloy was 1 × 10−5 at 1000 °C and 2 × 10−5 at 1100 °C, while AlCrMoTaTi alloy had Al activity of 3.63 × 10−6 at 1000 °C and 4.99 × 10−6 at 1100 °C. Obviously, NV1 alloy possessed much higher Al activities at both temperature than those of AlCrMoTaTi alloy, which was claimed to be able to form a protective Al2O3 layer, but no protective Al2O3 layer was found on NV1 alloy in present study. This work clearly demonstrates that the formation of CrTaO4-based oxide dominated the oxidation behaviour and attributed to parabolic mass gain behaviours at 1100 °C. However, protection from CrTaO4-based oxide could not fully prevent the ingestion of oxygen and nitrogen, and the increase of testing duration enabled changes in weight gain behaviours due to further internal oxidation and nitridation. Previous study on RHEAs/RCCAs even suggested cracked oxide at the corners of the sample could affect the weight gain behaviours,, which was not observed in present study.

At elevated temperatures, all metals react with hot gases. The most common high-temperature gaseous mixture is air, of which oxygen is the most reactive component. To avoid corrosion in air, carbon steel is limited to approximately 480 °C (900 °F). Oxidation resistance in stainless steels increases with additions of chromium, silicon, and aluminium. Small additions of cerium and yttrium increase the adhesion of the oxide layer on the surface. The addition of chromium remains the most common method to increase high-temperature corrosion resistance in stainless steels; chromium reacts with oxygen to form a chromium oxide scale, which reduces oxygen diffusion into the material. The minimum 10.5% chromium in stainless steels provides resistance to approximately 700 °C (1,300 °F), while 16% chromium provides resistance up to approximately 1,200 °C (2,200 °F). Type 304, the most common grade of stainless steel with 18% chromium, is resistant to approximately 870 °C (1,600 °F). Other gases, such as sulfur dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, chlorine, also attack stainless steel. source_paper.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the paper’s finding that Al addition promotes the formation of a protective alumina scale, and leverages the well-established reactive element effect—previously utilized in oxide dispersion-strengthened alloys—to further stabilize the scale.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: It proposes a strategic minor alloying modification (yttrium addition) to actively enhance oxide scale stability via formation of interfacial dispersoids, a mechanism not discussed in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A minor reactive element addition of yttrium to CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloys induces the in-situ formation of fine Y-rich oxide dispersoids at the metal/oxide interface, which alleviate interfacial stresses and prevent scale spallation during prolonged high-temperature oxidation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (with X = Al, Si, or Mn) produced by MA + SPS, where the Al-containing variant naturally forms a protective Al2O3 scale.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate a small amount (0.1–0.5 at.%) of yttrium into the alloy feedstock prior to mechanical alloying.
hypothesis.conditions: After standard MA + SPS processing, subject the Y-doped and undoped alloys to oxidation at >900 °C in an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere for roughly 100 hours.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation and dispersion of nanoscale Y-rich oxide particles at the metal/oxide interface.
hypothesis.mechanism: The reactive element (Y) segregates to the metal/oxide interface during high-temperature exposure and forms finely dispersed Y-rich oxides. These dispersoids act to pin the interface, reduce residual stresses by accommodating thermal expansion differences, and inhibit the propagation of defects that could lead to spallation. Since Al-containing alloys form Al2O3 initially, the addition of Y further stabilizes this scale. In contrast, alloys with X = Si or Mn, which do not predominantly form alumina, would not benefit as strongly from Y additions.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Y-doped CrFeCoNiAl alloys will display a more adherent and stable oxide scale, with reduced oxide scale thickness fluctuations, lower weight gain, and diminished interfacial cracking compared with undoped Al-containing alloys. The effect should be testably different from the behavior in Si- or Mn-containing alloys with or without Y.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped CrFeCoNiAl alloys processed under identical conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: Valid for MA + SPS processed HEAs subjected to oxidizing exposures above 900 °C; reactive element effects may depend on the precise Y concentration and alloy chemical complexity.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise optimum Y concentration and its distribution are not well established, and potential interactions with other alloy components may complicate the response.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate CrFeCoNiAl alloys with and without a 0.1–0.5 at.% Y addition using identical MA + SPS processing. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at >900 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scale using cross-sectional TEM/SEM and measure interfacial strain/stresses (via XRD or nanoindentation at the interface) and oxidation weight gain.
measurements: Distribution and size of Y-rich oxide dispersoids (TEM/EDS)
Interfacial stress and oxide/metal adhesion (XRD, nanoindentation)
Oxide scale morphology and thickness (cross-sectional TEM/SEM)
Overall oxidation weight gain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped Al-containing HEA does not exhibit a significant reduction in interfacial stress, a more uniform and adherent protective oxide scale, and lower weight gain compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding.

top3.builds_on: the paper’s finding that Al-rich oxides form the stable protective phase (Al2O3) at 900 °C, extended by incorporating high-entropy effects such as sluggish diffusion to ensure a uniform Al distribution.
top3.what_is_new: It explicitly integrates the high-entropy alloy’s slow diffusion kinetics into the mechanism of oxide formation, proposing that controlled Al enrichment uniquely yields a resilient oxide scale in HEAs—an aspect not addressed in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled Al enrichment in CrFeCoNiX (X = Al) high-entropy alloys leverages the sluggish diffusion intrinsic to HEAs to promote a continuous, coherent Al2O3 scale that resists spallation at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a baseline (lower) Al content.
hypothesis.intervention: Increase the Al content moderately relative to the other elements to enhance the available Al reservoir.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or Na2SO4 + NaCl corrosive atmospheres.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A continuous, uniform Al2O3 layer at the metal/oxide interface.
hypothesis.mechanism: In high-entropy alloys, the sluggish diffusion characteristic promotes a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements. With enhanced Al content, the outward diffusion of Al becomes a controlled process, allowing for the formation of a protective Al2O3 film that has an optimal Pilling–Bedworth ratio (between 1 and 2). This controlled, slow oxidation minimizes localized depletion and prevents the formation of mixed, unstable oxides, thereby reducing thermal stresses that cause cracking or spallation. This contrasts with conventional alloys where rapid Al depletion might lead to non-protective oxide formation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Alloys with enhanced Al content will show a significantly lower oxide spallation area and reduced mass loss (relative to the baseline alloy) due to more coherent and adherent Al2O3 scale formation.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys with standard (lower) Al content or with X = Mn/Si, which tend to form mixed oxides that spall more readily.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable for single- or multiphase solid-solution states exposed to temperatures >900 °C in both pure oxidative and salt-containing corrosive environments.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact threshold of Al enrichment and the quantitative improvement in spallation resistance are uncertain and need to be established experimentally within the context of HEA diffusion kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of CrFeCoNiX alloys: one with baseline Al content and one with moderately enhanced Al content. Expose polished specimens to 900 °C in a controlled Na2SO4 + NaCl environment for 60 hours.
measurements: Spallation area fraction and oxide morphology via SEM
Phase identification of the oxide scales via XRD
Mass change measurements before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enriched alloys do not exhibit a more continuous, coherent Al2O3 layer and show similar or higher oxide spallation and mass loss relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that oxidation behavior is element-specific and guided by intrinsic redox potentials is extended by considering Si’s well-known passivation via the formation of an amorphous oxide.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes exploiting strategic Si segregation to deliberately form a glassy, self-sealing oxide layer at high temperatures—a mechanism not addressed in the paper, which focused on Mn and Al oxidation behavior at lower oxidation temperatures.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiSi alloys, promoting nanoscale Si segregation via controlled heat treatment should enable the rapid formation of an amorphous, continuous SiO₂ sublayer at the metal/oxide interface during exposure above 900 °C, thereby suppressing further oxidation and spallation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CrFeCoNiSi high-entropy alloy prepared by arc melting, homogenized and recrystallized to yield a uniform solid solution with Si as the minor alloying element.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a tailored heat-treatment protocol (e.g., a subsolvus anneal at ~950 °C for a short duration) designed to drive subtle nanoscale segregation of Si toward the surface or grain boundaries, without forming deleterious crystalline phases.
hypothesis.conditions: Subsequent exposure in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged durations.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An interfacial, amorphous SiO₂ sublayer that is continuous and conformal over the alloy, acting as a diffusion barrier.
hypothesis.mechanism: Silicon has a strong tendency to form a viscous, glassy oxide (SiO₂) that is continuous and chemically inert. By promoting Si segregation near the surface, the early-stage oxidation leads to the nucleation of an ultrathin amorphous SiO₂ film that limits oxygen ingress and metal cation diffusion. This sublayer ‘pins’ subsequent oxide growth and accommodates thermal stresses, preventing cracking or spallation. Unlike the volatile oxides that might form from Mn or even layered oxides from Al, the SiO₂ layer is intrinsically stable because of its low defect mobility and passivating characteristics as predicted by Pilling–Bedworth concepts.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional processing, the Si-treated alloy will form a thin (likely <10 nm), uniform, and adherent SiO₂ sublayer that substantially reduces further oxidation and scale spallation. The protective effect is expected to enhance oxidation resistance, though the precise improvement magnitude is moderately uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Mn or Al) processed without pre‐segregation heat treatment, which tend to develop multilayered oxide scales that are prone to cracking or spallation.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to single-phase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiSi alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; the beneficial effect is valid as long as the processing does not induce deleterious phase separation.
hypothesis.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimum heat-treatment parameters required to achieve effective Si segregation without compromising bulk phase stability. The exact thickness and defect density of the SiO₂ sublayer must be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiSi alloy samples: one undergoing the targeted pre-oxidation heat treatment to promote Si segregation and one processed conventionally. Expose both sets to an oxidative atmosphere above 900 °C for a fixed time. Characterize the surface via cross-sectional TEM, APT, and XPS to identify the presence, continuity, and composition of the SiO₂ sublayer, and perform adhesion tests (e.g., thermal cycling).
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the surface SiO₂ layer (via TEM and APT)
Chemical composition and bonding state of the oxide (via XPS)
Spallation and adhesion behavior under thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated alloy does not exhibit a significantly more continuous and adherent SiO₂ layer—and if its oxidation resistance is not notably improved compared to the baseline—the hypothesis is refuted.

The surface of titanium and of titanium-rich alloys oxidizes immediately upon exposure to air to form a thin passivation layer of titanium oxide, mostly titanium dioxide. This layer makes it resistant to further corrosion, aside from gradual growth of the oxide layer, thickening to ~25 nm after several years in air. This protective layer makes it suitable for use even in corrosive environments such as sea water. Titanium can be anodized to produce a thicker passivation layer. As with many other metals, this layer causes thin-film interference which makes the metal surface appear colored, with the thickness of the passivation layer directly effecting the color produced.

expert_context.question: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: the paper’s detailed investigation of oxidation-driven compositional inversion and element-specific diffusion (as shown by APT and XANES) and uses the idea of controlled pre-oxidation to manipulate surface chemistry as a means to stabilize the oxide layer.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled Pre‐Oxidation to Tailor Surface Composition and Establish a Protective Nucleation Template
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CrFeCoNiX alloy (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a homogeneous, well-sintered FCC state prepared by conventional melting, homogenization, and recrystallization, with a mirror-polished surface.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the alloy surface to a controlled pre‐oxidation treatment in a mildly reducing or weakly oxidizing atmosphere at an intermediate temperature (≈850 °C) before exposing the alloy to a full oxidative/corrosive environment above 900 °C.
hypothesis.conditions: A two-step thermal treatment: initial pre‐oxidation at approximately 850 °C in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., low oxygen partial pressure or slightly reducing) followed by exposure at >900 °C in an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An engineered gradient layer at the surface wherein faster-diffusing elements are partially depleted and slower-oxidizing, passivating elements (such as Cr and Al or Si) are enriched, thereby forming an optimal nucleation template for the subsequent formation of a coherent protective oxide.
hypothesis.mechanism: During the pre-oxidation step under controlled atmospheres, faster diffusing species (e.g., Mn) are preferentially removed from the extreme surface, leading to an enrichment of elements like Cr and Al (or Si) that form slower-growing, more adherent oxides. This tailored surface composition then acts as an ideal template during the subsequent exposure at >900 °C, promoting the nucleation and growth of a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer with improved structural integrity. The graded compositional transition reduces the thermal expansion mismatch and stress accumulation that can lead to spallation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The alloy samples that undergo the controlled pre‐oxidation treatment will develop a graded, coherent oxide scale with reduced thickness and improved adhesion (i.e., less cracking or spallation) compared to samples that are directly oxidized at >900 °C without the pre-treatment.
hypothesis.baseline: Identical CrFeCoNiX alloy samples subjected directly to oxidation at >900 °C without any pre‐oxidation step.
hypothesis.boundary: The pre‐oxidation treatment must be carefully optimized for temperature, duration, and atmosphere. Excessively aggressive pre‐oxidation might lead to a porous or excessively depleted surface, while insufficient treatment may not yield the desired compositional gradient.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal pre‐oxidation conditions (temperature, time, atmosphere) that result in the desired surface enrichment and how robust the templated layer is during subsequent high-temperature exposure remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one subjected to a controlled pre‐oxidation treatment at ≈850 °C under a mildly reducing/low-oxygen atmosphere followed by full oxidation at >900 °C, and another set directly oxidized at >900 °C. Analyze the oxide layers using cross-sectional TEM, APT, and XPS to assess the oxide’s thickness, composition gradient, and structural coherence. Perform thermal cycling tests to check for spallation.
measurements: Surface compositional profiles and oxide layer structure (via TEM and APT)
Oxide phase composition (using XPS and XRD)
Mechanical integrity through thermal cycling and SEM imaging of surface cracks/spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples undergoing pre‐oxidation do not exhibit a significantly more graded and coherent oxide layer with reduced cracking/spallation compared to the as-oxidized samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: The Effect of Copper on the Microstructure, Wear and Corrosion Resistance of CoCrCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Manufactured by Powder Metallurgy.

top3.builds_on: This builds on the general understanding of oxidation in HEAs and passivation behavior (as described in the background texts on passivation and the Pilling–Bedworth ratio) and extends it by using controlled, low-level silicon doping to tailor the oxide scale composition.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically tests a silicon substitution strategy at a lower doping level (≈3 at.%) that minimizes silicide formation while promoting an amorphous SiO2 phase within a Cr2O3 matrix, a mechanism not explored in the original copper-doping study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Reducing the silicon doping level in CrFeCoNi from 0 to about 3 at.% will promote the in situ formation of a nanoscale, amorphous SiO2 component that intermixes with the protective Cr2O3 scale, thereby enhancing strain accommodation and adhesion at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) in a single-phase solid-solution state with no silicon.
hypothesis.intervention: Substitute about 3 at.% of one of the base elements (e.g., partial replacement of Ni) with silicon to form CrFeCoNiSi (≈3 at.% Si).
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure to a high-temperature oxidative or corrosive atmosphere (e.g., oxygen-rich gas with trace water vapor) at temperatures above 900 °C under cyclic thermal loading.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A composite oxide scale in which a thin, amorphous, dispersed SiO2 phase is embedded in and at the metal/oxide interface with a continuous Cr2O3 layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: Thermodynamic calculations and CALPHAD assessments (from established literature on oxidation and passivation [TXT::wikipedia::Passivation_(chemistry)::004, TXT::wikipedia::Pilling–Bedworth_ratio::001]) indicate that at low (<3 at.%) silicon levels, the alloy remains in a solid solution without triggering silicide formation. At high temperature, silicon has a high oxygen affinity and oxidizes preferentially to form an amorphous silica phase that mixes with Cr2O3. The amorphous SiO2 phase can accommodate thermal expansion mismatches and deflect cracking, thereby reducing spallation of the oxide scale.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Si-doped CrFeCoNiSi alloy will form a thinner, more adherent, and crack-resistant composite oxide scale with lower spallation rates compared to the undoped CrFeCoNi alloy. The improvement is expected to be significant (qualitatively >30–50% reduction in defect density) though the precise magnitude requires experimental quantification.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped CrFeCoNi HEA tested under the same high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: Temperature ≥900 °C in oxidizing atmospheres typical of high-temperature industrial or aerospace environments, with cyclic thermal stresses applied.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction and distribution of the amorphous SiO2 phase and its effect on overall mechanical compliance is uncertain and needs experimental validation; thermodynamic predictions support the mechanism at ~3 at.% silicon but detailed kinetics remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples via identical processing routes: one set of undoped CrFeCoNi and one set with 3 at.% Si substitution (CrFeCoNiSi). Subject both sets to cyclic oxidation treatments at ~950 °C in a controlled oxygen-rich atmosphere. Perform cross-sectional analysis using TEM/SEM combined with EDS and XRD to evaluate oxide scale thickness, phase distribution, and crack density. Additionally, conduct thermal shock tests to assess spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (via TEM/SEM)
Phase identification and distribution (using XRD and EDS)
Crack density and spallation incidence (thermal shock and adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped alloy shows no statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity, adhesion, and reduction of cracking/spallation compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.

top3.builds_on: the paper’s findings of oxide instability driven by excessive Mn oxidation and uncontrolled diffusion (PMC8346963, sections 3.1–3.2) and on diffusion-based segregation principles in alloy systems.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific, two-step thermal treatment to induce controlled nanoscale Cr enrichment and thus form a graded, dual-layer oxide structure with improved adhesion—a novel approach not previously reported in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloys, a tailored two-step thermal treatment can induce controlled nanoscale Cr enrichment at grain boundaries, thereby promoting the in situ formation of an adherent Cr2O3 sublayer beneath a modified Mn-rich oxide and mitigating the spallation observed at temperatures above 900 °C.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A homogenous, single-phase CrFeCoNiMn HEA with a uniformly distributed FCC structure produced by conventional processing.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment: first, a short-duration low-temperature annealing (e.g., around 800 °C) to initiate slight Cr segregation toward grain boundaries without full phase separation, followed by a rapid ramp to the oxidation temperature (≥900 °C).
hypothesis.conditions: Oxidation in synthetic air (or corrosive atmosphere) at temperatures ≥900 °C for durations from 12 to 48 h.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded oxide scale consisting of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 sublayer (formed at Cr-enriched grain boundaries) that mechanically anchors an outer Mn-rich oxide layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: The controlled two-step thermal treatment exploits the differential diffusion rates of Cr and Mn. The initial low-temperature step induces mild Cr enrichment at grain boundaries without triggering full phase separation. Once the oxidation temperature is reached, the Cr-enriched regions preferentially form a stable Cr2O3 sublayer (which possesses a high Pilling–Bedworth ratio and good mechanical integrity). This sublayer acts as a robust diffusion barrier and mechanical anchor that mitigates the spallation typically observed from Mn-rich, less-adherent oxide formation. The resulting graded oxide scale exhibits improved resistance to cracking and delamination.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared with a baseline CrFeCoNiMn alloy processed without the two-step treatment, the treated sample will form a dual-layer oxide scale with a continuous, well-adherent Cr2O3 sublayer (documented via cross-sectional SEM/TEM and EDS mapping), reduced overall mass gain, and fewer spallation events under thermal cycling.
hypothesis.baseline: A conventionally processed homogenous CrFeCoNiMn alloy that develops unstable, spalling mixed Mn-rich oxides upon high-temperature exposure as reported in PMC8346963.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to equiatomic CrFeCoNiMn HEAs where the two-step thermal treatment can be applied without triggering detrimental phase separation, with oxidation tests performed at ≥900 °C in synthetic air for 12–48 h.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The feasibility and reproducibility of inducing controlled nanoscale Cr segregation without unwanted phase separation require further experimental optimization; precise gradient parameters (e.g., temperature differential and annealing duration) may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiMn samples: one subjected to the tailored two-step thermal treatment (low-temperature anneal followed by rapid ramp-up to ≥900 °C) and one maintained as a homogeneous control. Expose both sets to oxidation at 900 °C for 48 h.
measurements: TEM/SEM with EDS mapping to detect nanoscale Cr enrichment and verify the presence of a continuous Cr2O3 sublayer
Mass gain and oxidation kinetics measurements
Adhesion tests (e.g., thermal cycling or scratch tests) to assess the mechanical integrity of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated sample does not display a graded oxide scale with a continuous Cr2O3 sublayer and does not show a significant improvement in oxidation resistance and reduced spallation compared to the homogeneous control, the hypothesis is falsified.

This approach, involving examination of elemental distributions within a two-nanometer thick slice of interest at the specimen’s center, allowed for enhanced visualization of distributions across the oxide/metal interface. These 2D slices in Fig. 3d from the reconstructions facilitate a clear differentiation of dominant regions, such as Cr-rich and Fe-rich zones, enabling the distinction between inner and outer oxide regions (refer to Figs. S5–S7 for further details). Furthermore, the region enriched in Ni shed light on the enrichment zone situated just beneath the oxide layer, prior to reaching the base alloy. The spatial distribution of Mn indicates varying degrees of dominance in certain outer regions, notably at the top-left and bottom-left corners (refer to Fig. 3d).

Conversely, when analyzing the top right corner (as depicted in Fig. 3f), where Co-rich islands are found, a significant variation emerges. In this region, the prevalence of Co and Fe is notably pronounced in the outer oxide, while Mn appears less abundant. Intriguingly, there’s a substantial discrepancy in the depth of the inner oxide and enrichment region when compared to the orthogonal corner (Fig. 3e). The Cr-rich inner oxide spans ~3 nm, whereas the Ni-rich interface extends to around 5 nm. This non-uniformity underscores the significance of examining oxidation from various angles and dimensions. We infer that given inherent surface elasticity, early oxidizing, and late oxidizing elements follow orthogonal diffusion paths and hence distribute differently on the surface. Despite the predictability of trends, controlling the direction of diffusion kinetics presents a more intricate challenge. These APT results provide evidence that PIP (Fig. 1a) can provide a degree of predictability for the oxidation and speciation process for an otherwise highly entropic (and chaotic) system. High-temperature corrosion is chemical deterioration of a material (typically a metal) as a result of heating. This non-galvanic form of corrosion can occur when a metal is subjected to a hot atmosphere containing oxygen, sulfur ("sulfidation"), or other compounds capable of oxidizing (or assisting the oxidation of) the material concerned. For example, materials used in aerospace, power generation, and even in car engines must resist sustained periods at high temperature, during which they may be exposed to an atmosphere containing the potentially highly-corrosive products of combustion. Some products of high-temperature corrosion can potentially be turned to the advantage of the engineer. The formation of oxides on stainless steels, for example, can provide a protective layer preventing further atmospheric attack, allowing for a material to be used for sustained periods at both room and high temperatures in hostile conditions. Such high-temperature corrosion products, in the form of compacted oxide layer glazes, prevent or reduce wear during high-temperature sliding contact of metallic (or metallic and ceramic) surfaces.
